summary: Formally defines Routing Backus-Naur Form, a variant of BNF already used by several routing area protocol specifications to describe message syntax. Sharing one defined notation makes related protocols easier to read and compare.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5511 writes down the rules of a notation that several routing protocol documents had been using without a formal definition. It says what the pieces of a rule are, what each of the six operators means, and how the operators bind together, which is where the old documents were ambiguous. It also says when a new protocol should use this notation and when it should use a broader one.

questions: what does ::= mean in rfc message syntax
subtitle: A formal definition of the Backus-Naur notation that routing protocol specifications have been using without one.

tldr.problem: Several routing area protocols describe their message formats in a variant of Backus-Naur Form, but no formal definition of that variant exists, so the same text can be read in more than one way and implementers have to guess.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives the variant a name, Routing BNF, and defines it: the kinds of rule, the six operators, the editorial conventions and the order in which the operators bind. It also says where the notation may and may not be used, and how a specification should be written to avoid the ambiguity the RFC found in the existing documents.
tldr.outcome: The result is that the many documents already written in this notation can be read unambiguously, and that new extensions to those protocols can be written in a way machines can check. The RFC notes that no automated validation tool existed when it was written.

facts.label: Precedence order
facts.value: Objects and constructs, repetition, grouping and optional, concatenation, alternative

facts.label: Automated validation tools
facts.value: None known at the time of writing

today: RFC 5511 is a Proposed Standard from April 2009 and is neither obsoleted nor updated. It names the notation Routing BNF and gives it a formal definition, so that the routing area documents already written in it can be read unambiguously, and it points readers who want a formally specified and broader form of BNF to RFC 5234.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Backus-Naur Form has been used to specify the message formats of several protocols within the Routing Area of the IETF. Those specifications are not based on any specific formal definition of BNF, and they differ slightly from the definitions provided in other places.

It is clearly valuable to have a formal definition of the syntax-defining language that is used. It would be possible to convert all the existing specifications to use an established specification of BNF, for example Augmented BNF, but that would require a lot of work, and there is a further obstacle. In ABNF the terminals are integers, that is characters or bytes, while in the BNF form used to define message formats the terminals are objects, some kind of message element rather than an individual byte or character, or entire messages. Converting the existing specifications to an established BNF specification would therefore also require extensions to that specification.

The variant used by the specifications in question, which is similar to a subset of Extended BNF, is consistent and has only a small number of constructs. This document therefore provides a specification of that variant, names it Routing BNF, and makes it available for new protocols. A formal definition also allows the formal definitions used in future documents to be verified automatically.
sections.plainLanguage: Several routing protocols write their message formats in a notation that nobody had written down properly. This RFC writes it down, so that two people reading the same rule cannot reasonably read it two different ways.

sections.title: Where the Notation Is Used
sections.content:
The first notable use of the variant is in the specification of the Resource Reservation Protocol, RSVP. RSVP was extended for use in Multiprotocol Label Switching networks to provide signalling for traffic engineering, and that extension was developed further for use as the signalling protocol in Generalized MPLS networks.

Each of those uses of RSVP gave rise to a large number of specifications of protocol extensions that provide additional features over and above the base documents, and each new feature is defined in its own document using the common variant of BNF. New protocols have also been specified in the same variant, partly because their developers were familiar with the BNF used by RSVP, and partly because of the overlap between the protocols, especially with respect to the network objects they control and operate. Notable among these additional protocols are the Link Management Protocol, for which further extension documents also use the same variant, and the Path Computation Element Protocol, again with extension documents in the same variant.

As for applicability, RBNF is primarily applicable to the protocols just listed. It may be used to help interpret the pre-existing RFCs that use it, and it should be used in the specification of extensions to those protocols. It could also be used for new protocols, which is most appropriate for protocols closely related to those that already use RBNF: PCEP is closely related to RSVP-TE, and when it was developed, the PCE working group chose the same form of BNF as the RSVP-TE specifications already used. If a wholly new protocol is being developed that is not related to a protocol that already uses RBNF, the working group should consider carefully whether to use RBNF or a more formally specified and broader form such as ABNF. Using RBNF to specify extensions to protocols that do not already use it is not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The notation came from RSVP, spread through its traffic engineering extensions into Generalized MPLS, and was then adopted by two later protocols. New documents should use it when they extend those protocols, and should think twice before using it for something unrelated.

sections.title: Rules: Objects, Constructs and Messages
sections.content:
The basic building blocks of BNF are rules and operators. At its simplest, a rule in this context is a protocol object that would traditionally be defined by a bit diagram in the protocol specification. Further and more complex rules are constructed by combining other rules using operators, and the most complex rule is the message, which is constructed from an organisation of protocol objects as specified by the operators.

An RBNF specification consists of a sequence of rule definitions using the operators. One rule may be constructed from a set of other rules using operators, and the order of definition of rules does not matter: the subordinate rules may be defined first and then used in subsequent definitions, or the top-level rules may be defined first followed by the definitions of the subordinate rules. Rule definitions are read left to right on any line, and the lines are read top to bottom on the page, which becomes particularly important when considering sequences of rules and operators.

No semantics should be assumed from special characters used in rule names. It would be wrong, for example, to assume that a rule carries a decimal number because its name begins or ends with the letter d, though individual specifications may choose to assign rule names in any way that makes the human interpretation of the rule easier. All rule names are enclosed by angle brackets, may include any printable characters, and must not include tabs or line breaks.

Three kinds of rule are distinguished, and each has a customary naming style. An object is the most basic, indivisible rule, and its definition is derived from its context; objects are typically named in uppercase and do not usually use spaces within the name, favouring underbars. A construct is a rule constructed from other rules using operators; constructs are named in lowercase, although capitals are commonly used to indicate acronyms, and spaces and hyphens are used between words within names. A message is the final objective, a rule constructed from objects and constructs using operators; the only syntactic difference between a message and a construct is that no other rule is typically constructed from a message, and messages are typically named in title case.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule is either a single indivisible piece of a protocol, a piece built out of other pieces, or a whole message. The three are written with different styles of name, but the naming is a convention rather than a rule, and nothing may be assumed from the characters in a name.

sections.title: The Six Operators
sections.content:
Operators are used to build constructs and messages from objects and constructs. Assignment is written as a colon, a colon and an equal sign, and it means that the named construct or message on the left-hand side is set equal to the right-hand side. The left-hand side and the assignment operator must be present on the same line.

Concatenation is a sequence of objects and constructs, usually separated by spaces, which must be present in the order specified. The objects in a sequence may be separated by line breaks.

Optional presence is written in square brackets. The optional objects or constructs may be present or absent within the assignment, and unless indicated as optional, objects and constructs are mandatory and must be present. The optional operator can also be nested to give a hierarchical dependency of presence: in a construction of the form <construct> ::= <MAND> [ <OPT_1> [ <OPT_2> ] ], the object OPT_2 can only be present if OPT_1 is also present. The set of objects and constructs within the same pair of square brackets is treated as a unit, so when multiple are included within the same pair they must all be included when one is, unless nested square brackets are used.

Alternatives are written with the pipe symbol between the objects or constructs that are alternatives, and either one rule or the other must be present. The use of explicit grouping is recommended to avoid confusion, since implicit grouping using line breaks is often used but gives rise to potential misinterpretation and should be avoided in new definitions. One particular form is not allowed in new documents: a construct with two alternatives, each of which has two members, because it could be read either as requiring a member or as making one optional. It must be presented using grouping or an intermediary construct instead.

Repetition is written as three dots and means that the preceding object, intermediate construct or construct may repeat. A set of zero or more objects or constructs is achieved by combining it with the optional concept, and a sequence can also be encoded by building a recursive construct using the alternative operator. Repetition can also be applied to a component of an assignment to indicate optional repetition of that component, as in a definition that allows zero or more instances of an alternative group.

Grouping is written with round brackets enclosing a set of objects, constructs and operators, and says that they are to be treated together. The notation is not mandatory but is recommended for clarity, because the precedence rules mean that grouping is not needed for the formal interpretation of the representation, while it does make the notation easier to parse unambiguously. Either grouping or an intermediate construct must be used for multi-alternates.
sections.plainLanguage: Six symbols do all the work: equals signs define a rule, spaces put things in order, brackets mark what is optional, the vertical bar offers a choice, three dots mean repeated, and round brackets say that what is inside is to be read as a unit.

sections.title: Editorial Conventions
sections.content:
White space between operators, objects and constructs is ignored, but should be used for readability. Line breaks within an assignment are ignored as well, and should be used for readability.

Line breaks are often used to imply grouping within the precedence rules, but explicit grouping or intermediary constructs should be used in new definitions, because the line break habit is open to misinterpretation. A line break must not be present between the left-hand side of an assignment and the assignment operator, and new assignments must begin on a new line.

The ordering of objects and constructs in an assignment is explicit. Protocol specifications may opt to state that ordering is only recommended, in which case the elements of a list of objects and constructs may be received in any order.
sections.plainLanguage: Spaces and line breaks do not change the meaning, but the RFC asks writers to use round brackets when they want a reader to see a group, because a line break on its own can be misread.

sections.title: Precedence
sections.content:
Precedence is the main opportunity for confusion in the use of this notation, because the use of alternatives mixed with concatenations can give rise to different interpretations of the same text. Although precedence can be deduced from a proper reading of the notation using the rules already given, authors are strongly recommended to use grouping and ordering to avoid cases where the reader would otherwise be required to understand the precedence rules. Automated readers are required to parse rules correctly with or without this use of grouping.

The mechanisms have a fixed precedence, from highest, meaning binding tightest, to lowest: objects and constructs; repetition; grouping and optional; concatenation; and alternative.

An example of the confusion can be found in the RSVP specification. A definition written as <flow descriptor list> ::= <empty> | <flow descriptor list> <flow descriptor> can be read in two ways, and the implementer must decide which is intended: either the list is empty or it is a list followed by one descriptor, or the list is empty or not and is always followed by a descriptor. The line break may be interpreted as implying grouping, but that is not an explicit rule. The precedence rules say that concatenation has higher precedence than the alternative operator, so the text should be read in the first sense. The same applies to a second definition from the same section, where the flow specification and the filter specification belong together in the first alternative, and to any similar case in a new document, where the use of explicit grouping or intermediary constructs is strongly recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: When a rule mixes choices with sequences, the reader has to know which binds tighter. Here the answer is fixed: a single piece binds tightest, then repetition, then brackets and round brackets, then sequence, and the choice between alternatives binds loosest.

sections.title: Automated Validation
sections.content: RBNF would be appropriate for verification using automated validation tools. Such tools need to be able to check for close conformance to the rules expressed in this document to be useful for verifying new documents, but should also be able to parse RBNF as it is used in existing RFCs. The RFC notes that no tools are known at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the notation is now written down, a program could check that a specification follows it. The RFC says no such program existed when it was written.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document does not define any network behaviour, and it neither introduces nor seeks to solve any security issue. It notes that clear and unambiguous protocol specifications reduce the likelihood of incompatible or defective implementations that might be exploited in security attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes what goes on the network. The RFC argues only that a specification people read the same way is less likely to produce an implementation with a flaw in it.

viz.caption: THE SIX OPERATORS AND HOW THEY ARE WRITTEN

items.label: Assignment
items.desc: The named construct or message on the left is set equal to the right-hand side. The left-hand side and the operator must be on the same line.

items.label: Concatenation
items.desc: A sequence of objects and constructs, which must be present in the order specified.

items.label: Optional presence
items.desc: The contents may be present or absent. Anything not marked optional is mandatory, and the brackets can be nested.

items.label: Alternatives
items.desc: Either one rule or the other must be present.

items.label: Repetition
items.desc: The preceding object, intermediate construct or construct may repeat.

items.label: Grouping
items.desc: The enclosed objects, constructs and operators are treated together. Recommended for clarity.

items.title: Object
items.text: The most basic indivisible rule, defined by its context. Named in uppercase, with underbars rather than spaces, for example SENDER_TEMPLATE.

items.title: Construct
items.text: A rule built from other rules with operators. Named in lowercase, with capitals for acronyms and spaces or hyphens between words.

items.title: Message
items.text: The final objective, built from objects and constructs. Named in title case, and no other rule is typically built from a message.
